title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
summary: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

title: Bridge: Database-Grounded Interactive Disambiguation for Text-to-SQL
summary: Ambiguity remains a persistent challenge in text-to-SQL, where an underspecified natural-language question may admit multiple plausible SQL interpretations. Recent work attempts to recover the user's intended interpretation through iterative clarification, but typically relies heavily on LLM parametric knowledge for ad hoc reasoning, leading to limited ambiguity-resolution effectiveness and high LLM cost. We further observe that many ambiguity errors stem from ambiguous column grounding, which remains poorly handled. Therefore, we propose Bridge, a database-grounded disambiguation framework built on an existing iterative protocol. Bridge supplies the LLM's ambiguity detection with offline-distilled knowledge about potential ambiguity relations among columns in the target database. Offline, Bridge constructs a Column Ambiguity Graph by first identifying potentially ambiguous column pairs using complementary database-grounded signals, followed by LLM-based verification. Online, columns and values mentioned in a previous incorrect SQL prediction are used as anchors to retrieve alternatives from the Column Ambiguity Graph and an offline-constructed value similarity index, respectively. The results are integrated for further pruning and consolidated for subsequent ambiguity detection. Extensive experiments on BIRD-dev without the benchmark-provided evidence show that, at comparable LLM cost, Bridge outperforms the strongest baseline by 11.60% in execution accuracy and improves the recall and precision of column usage in the final SQL by 5.25% and 12.37%, respectively.

title: Query Processing with eBPF-Offload on Computational Storage
summary: The idea of pushing computation to storage devices has been explored for decades. In recent years, research has focused on computational storage, i.e., devices that allow a host to execute functions as I/O commands on local data. Today, the NVMe and SNIA computational storage standards share an execution model in which the host invokes functions on the device, on data that the host has moved into device memory. Both standards single out eBPF as a format for functions offloaded by the host. In this paper, we study whether this form of computational storage is a good match for query processing. We present the design and implementation of Delilah, a prototype based on an open-hardware device that implements the standard execution model on an actual device and runs eBPF programs calling device-resident functions. As an initial step, we hand-coded a portion of SSB Q3.3 for execution on the device, aiming to integrate computational storage with a database system's storage manager. The series of experiments that we ran showed that offloading gains little over host execution, execution degenerates into column-at-a-time processing, and time is spent staging and moving data in device memory. Because these roadblocks stem from the execution model rather than from the query, we did not pursue integration further. We detail these limitations and lay the groundwork for a different computational storage model better aligned with data-intensive workloads.

title: MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into SQL queries over increasingly complex databases. However, widely used benchmarks evaluate questions independently, overlooking settings where earlier queries over the same database can supply joins or calculations for a new question. We introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) to measure the accuracy and cost of adapting historical SQL. HARE comprises 1,600 requests derived from a fixed pool of 823 verified queries across four datasets. Annotations record which components each request preserves and which edits it requires, distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial reuse. Our method, MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and mappings from domain concepts to schema elements. MEM-SQL uses a layer only if every requirement assigned to it has a match above that layer's threshold. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), MEM-SQL consults the schema only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges retrieved evidence insufficient. Across six language models on HARE, mean execution accuracy rises from 37.1% for Direct Generation without history to 50.0% for MEM-SQL, with 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency on average. Further analysis shows that requests reusing several verified queries remain a bottleneck, with accuracy falling from 56.7% to 29.7%, most sharply when reused components must be placed in a new query structure or combined with a shared join. Applying OSL to three other memory designs consistently reduces generation cost, while its accuracy benefit depends on the memory design. Verified history can thus make generation both more accurate and cheaper, but its value depends on the evidence retained and when the system consults the schema.

title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the WACCPD 2026 workshop (SC26 Workshops), November 15-20, 2026, Chicago, Illinois, USA
summary: Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance. GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends. We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs. The new SYCL backend comes within 3% of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to 1.75x and 2.17x on the A30 and up to 1.79x and 4.62x on an AMD Instinct MI210. On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPUs, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend. Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.

title: ProdPilot: A Layered Model Context Protocol System for Automated Production Readiness and Deployment of Vibe-Coded Projects
summary: AI-assisted development environments turn natural-language requests into working applications, yet the projects they produce often fail on their first deployment for operational reasons: credentials in source files, missing security middleware, no container definition, no health endpoint and no delivery pipeline. Automated repair of such defects usually relies on free-form model generation, which varies between runs and is seldom checked independently. This paper presents ProdPilot, a local Model Context Protocol server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production readiness rules, repairs violations through a bounded loop, gates the result and deploys it. Each rule is classified by what its fix requires: 28 fixes are fixed templates, 16 are filled with values extracted from the project and only 6 are written by the IDE agent's model, so 88.0\% of the ruleset needs no model-written content, and across 499 real repositories 93.5\% of the violations found fall in those classes. A fix, however it was produced, is accepted only if the checker that flagged the rule now passes. In a full-chain run over 23 sample projects, template and extraction fixes that were applied as written passed their checkers in 87.6\% and 95.0\% of cases, and independent verification rejected 25 of the 237 fixes reported as applied. A deployability model trained on 684 real deployments ranks held-out projects at 0.909 ROC AUC, a gated project was deployed, smoke-tested and connected to an active CI/CD pipeline in 82 seconds, and the unchanged server worked from the IDE agents in VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf, where live agents resolved all six delegated rules on the first attempt under the same verification. ProdPilot itself runs no model.

title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

title: Time-Consistent Evaluation of Hierarchical Code Graphs for SWE Agents
summary:
Evaluating repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents requires strict separation between pre-existing repository knowledge and future code evolution, yet standard benchmarks frequently suffer from temporal contamination and prompt-level solution leakage. Building on the time-consistent benchmark protocol of Sun (2026), we enforce strict zero-leakage isolation across DragonFly in C++ and React in JavaScript/TypeScript, locking repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at historical cutoff commits $T_0$ and evaluating 100 post-$T_0$ pull requests across four prompt granularities: Minimal, Concise, Contextual, and Guided.
  Under this zero-leakage protocol, we conduct a matched evaluation of three context-augmentation regimes: (1) an unaugmented Baseline, (2) a flat syntax-level Tree-sitter AST graph, and (3) ServiceExplorer, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph capturing Level-1 system/package containers and Level-2 architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations spanning six foundation models across the MAI-Code Flash, Claude, and GPT-Sol families, ServiceExplorer consistently outperforms both Baseline and Tree-sitter AST across every model, repository, and prompt granularity ($+15.6\%$ to $+86.2\%$ relative $F_1$ lift, $p < 10^{-4}$), while tripling exact full-PR localization on DragonFly. Crucially, equipping an efficiency-tier or prior-generation model with ServiceExplorer consistently surpasses the unaugmented Baseline $F_1$ of the next-generation model across all evaluated families.

title: TailGuard-GDS: Tail-Safe Control of GPU Storage Data Movement
comment: This is a full-length research article. The manuscript is 35 pages and contains 14 figures and 17 tables, including the appendix. It is not under consideration elsewhere
summary:
AI runtimes move state between NVMe storage and GPU memory on critical paths. GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes host staging, yet our eight-H100 measurements show it is not consistently tail-optimal for semantically identical GPU-buffer operations. The preferred path varies with operation, request size, concurrency, placement, and resource contention; bandwidth and tail-latency winners can disagree. Frameworks specify what moves and when, while GPU I/O stacks expose mechanisms; neither combines phase semantics with measured tail behavior to choose a delivery plan.
  We present TailGuard-GDS, a runtime that selects a semantically equivalent plan per application phase. It profiles plans varying backend, request shape, and placement, minimizes GPU-visible tail latency under phase constraints, and revisits decisions as conditions change. Resource reuse keeps policy lookup and switching at microsecond-scale overhead.
  Integrated with PyTorch FSDP and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, TailGuard reduces FSDP step p95 by 18.4% and GPU-idle p95 by 25.3% versus the strongest fixed path. Across five eight-GPU ZeRO-3 workloads, step p95 falls 7.9-24.6% versus fixed host staging and 28.4-42.6% versus fixed GDS. Against tuned DeepSpeed AIO, TailGuard reduces step p95 by 5.6% and raises estimated throughput by 6.1%.

title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
comment: Accepted at the 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/SWE-rebench/trajectory-analyzer
summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

title: OrbitWeaver: LLM Agent Planning with Simulation Feedback for Optically Interconnected Orbital GPU Clusters
summary: Space-based data-center designs increasingly consider GPU computing formations connected by inter-satellite optical links. With limited neighboring connections, jobs assigned disjoint GPUs can still contend on shared relay paths. Rank placement and communication priorities jointly affect this contention and the readiness of downstream computation. We present OrbitWeaver, an offline large language model (LLM) agent planner that jointly optimizes rank placement and communication order. Guided by communication structure, execution dependencies, and simulation feedback, the agent constructs and refines plans that coordinate shared-link access with computation progress. This coordination reduces contention and dependency blocking, shortening mean job completion time (JCT). Simulation experiments on optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters show that OrbitWeaver reduces aggregate mean JCT by 6.2-33.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baselines CASSINI, Crux, and Symphony. These results demonstrate the value of LLM-guided planning for efficient concurrent computing in orbital GPU clusters.

title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
summary: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

title: The Exact Stabilization Time of Self-Stabilizing Coloring: Mean, Variance, and Distribution
summary: The worst-case stabilization time of a self-stabilizing algorithm usually says little about its typical behavior beyond the order of magnitude. This paper revisits the classical self-stabilizing $Delta+1$ coloring algorithm with vertices activated at random, one at a time (the random central daemon). Considering the number of color changes as a random variable, we study its mean, variance and, on several families of graphs, its exact distribution. The analysis rests on a reduction: a vertex changes color, at most once, exactly when it is not a local maximum of a uniformly random labeling of the vertices, maxima being taken among the neighbors that share its initial color (the monochrome initial configuration is the slowest case). What can be predicted depends on what is known of the graph. The degree distribution (the view at distance one) gives the mean. The variance needs the view at distance two, in particular the triangles, and the full law needs the whole graph. We give closed-form results, from monochrome and from uniformly random initial configurations, on paths, cycles, random trees, Erdős-R{é}nyi graphs and bipartite random graphs. From a monochrome start, the mean stays within a factor two of the worst case, whereas the variance ranges from zero (disjoint cliques) to order $n^2$ (the star on $n$ vertices)..

title: Beyond Source Code: Evaluating Natural Language Specifications for LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for C-to-Rust translation, yet existing approaches primarily rely on source code as input, leaving natural-language specifications of program behavior underexplored as an alternative or complementary representation. We hypothesize that direct code translation encourages LLMs to preserve C-specific implementation choices, producing Rust that may be functionally correct but unnecessarily verbose, reliant on unsafe constructs, and less idiomatic. We investigate this hypothesis by comparing three translation settings: code-only, specification-only, and code-and-specification. Using 300 C programs from the IBM CodeNet dataset, we evaluate GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o-mini on functional correctness, maintainability, complexity, idiomaticity, unsafe construct usage, and cost. Code-only translation achieves the highest test pass rate (98.6%) but often mirrors C's implementation patterns. In contrast, specification-only translation produces the most idiomatic and compact Rust, reducing unsafe blocks by approximately 6x and Clippy style warnings by 2.4x. However, using specifications without validation yields test pass rates as low as 86% with our best performing model. Adding an iterative test-based validation and refinement step for specifications raises this to a 95.3% test pass rate. Overall, specification-based translation consistently improves code quality relative to code-only translation, while code-and-specification offers the best balance between correctness (98.3% test pass rate) and maintainability. Our study systematically compares these translation settings, highlighting the trade-offs among specification quality, translation correctness, code quality, and computational cost.

title: Zero-SM NCCL: A Systematic Guide to Designing and Deploying SM-Free GPU Communication
summary: GPU communication libraries such as NCCL use Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) for data movement and synchronization, slowing overlapped computation at a cost that grows with interconnect bandwidth. We present Zero-SM NCCL, which communicates within and across scale-up domains without launching any SM kernel. It synchronizes through CUDA stream memory operations, moves data asynchronously with copy engines within a scale-up domain, and drives network RDMA from a stream-ordered CPU proxy. It supports data-movement collectives such as AllGather and AlltoAll, plus one-sided ncclPutSignal and ncclWaitSignal APIs. On GB200 NVL72 and B200 NVL8 systems, Zero-SM collectives reach up to 1.36x higher AllGather bandwidth than NCCL's legacy SM-based kernels and cut the median slowdown of overlapped GEMMs from 33% to 4%, at a higher latency per operation. In Megatron-LM training, they accelerate FSDP by up to 3.5%, and one-sided puts accelerate pipeline parallelism by up to 15%. Zero-SM communication is not a universal win, however. Through an end-to-end study across models and parallelism strategies, we show that it pays off for large transfers in GPU-bound workloads and for deep pipelines with large bubbles, but loses on small messages and host-bound workloads. We distill these findings into guidelines for enabling zero-SM communication in NCCL and building it into other libraries.

title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to GREENS 2027 (11th International Workshop on Green and Sustainable Software, co-located with ICSE 2027). Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24016482
summary: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.

title: Multi-GPU Tridiagonal Partition Algorithm
comment: 3 pages, 3 tables, Mathematical Modelling and Computational Physics 2026 international conference (MMCP'2026), Dubna, Russia
summary: This paper presents a multi-GPU version and a multi-GPU recursive version of the parallel partition method for systems of linear algebraic equations with tridiagonal coefficient matrices and their implementations in CUDA. Computational experiments on one and two GPU cards, for different system sizes and with different number of recursive steps are conducted. The results are analyzed and discussed.

title: SZZBench: Controlled Git Histories with Explicit Oracles for Diagnosing SZZ Implementations
summary: The SZZ algorithm traces a bug-fixing commit back to the commits that introduced the bug. Its labels underlie defect-prediction data sets and many mining software repositories studies. SZZ implementations are mostly evaluated against oracles mined from real projects. Such oracles are realistic, but each case mixes the history factors that make an implementation succeed or fail, and an aggregate score cannot show why. We present SZZBench, a tool that shows why: it generates ordinary Git repositories from declarative scenarios with explicit oracles, scores the predictions of any SZZ implementation under declared evaluation policies, and reads each result against 26 naive baselines, such as always answering the second commit. SZZBench also checks the declarations of new scenarios, such as the tier, against the results of the naive baselines. Currently, SZZBench ships 279 scenarios in 17 categories and adapters for four SZZ tools. Running these tools in nine configurations without changing their code, we find that PyDriller passes 161 scenarios and a rule that always answers the second commit passes 160, yet only 97 scenarios are passed by both: the two succeed on different scenarios, which the number of passed scenarios hides and the per-scenario results reveal. SZZBench is available at https://github.com/higolab/SZZBench.

title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 6 tables. Equal contribution from first two authors. Code: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aboleth
summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.

title: DesignSpecs: A DESIGN.md Dataset of Visual Design Specifications for AI Agents
summary: While AI agents increasingly generate and modify user interfaces, they rarely rely on a visual design specification for a certain project. The DESIGN.md format, which originated from Google's AI design tool Stitch and which was open-sourced in April 2026, addresses this gap by describing a visual identity through design tokens (such as named colors, text styles) and Markdown prose. To our knowledge, no large-scale research dataset of such design specification files exists. We present DesignSpecs, a dataset of 36,906 DESIGN.md files from 15,794 public, non-fork GitHub repositories, representing 17,240 unique file contents. We collected 613,207 files named DESIGN.md in October 2026. Because the same file name also denotes architectural plans and other design documents, we filtered those with YAML front matter, a design-system name, at least one recognized design token, and zero errors under the official linter. Our JSON Lines dataset provides file-level and deduplicated views of the original Markdown, links files to repositories, paths, and commits, and is released with related scripts. We outline research opportunities on visual design knowledge and design-aware AI agents. Dataset is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jl-wei/DesignSpecs

title: BPU-SpikeMM:Exact Matrix Multiplication via Spatio-Temporal Spike Encoding on Real Neuromorphic Hardware
summary: Matrix multiplication is the dominant computational kernel in deep learning, yet its growing scale strains conventional von Neumann hardware in energy efficiency and bandwidth. Neuromorphic architectures offer a promising alternative, but mathematical equivalence between matrix multiplication and spiking computation does not guarantee direct execution on real neuromorphic hardware, as the specific hardware paradigm may still require additional data recovery, bit-weight reconstruction, or state readout after neuromorphic execution. This paper presents BPU-SpikeMM (Brain Processing Unit-based Spike Matrix Multiplication), an exact spatio-temporal spike encoding framework for matrix multiplication on real neuromorphic hardware. We prove the exact equivalence of spike-encoded matrix multiplication under the BPU execution paradigm, distinguish mathematical equivalence from native direct-readout equivalence on BPU hardware, and build a spatio-temporal offloading pipeline supporting multiple encoding schemes. Furthermore, we extend the framework to a multi-dimensional encoding design space and evaluate the applicability of different encodings on real BPU hardware in terms of correctness, temporal resource cost, spatial resource cost, and event-driven metrics. The results confirm native direct-readout equivalence across all evaluated encoding schemes and show that their applicability to BPU execution depends on joint trade-offs among temporal cost, spatial resource consumption, and event activity.

title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup
summary: Modern coding agents rely on establishing executable software environments before they can perform software engineering tasks such as testing, debugging, and patch validation. Existing setup agents typically control progress at either single-command or whole-script granularity, making recovery either too local to remove polluted state or too coarse to preserve useful progress. We present HerAgent (Harness EnviRonment Setup Agent), a block-level harness for coding-agent environment setup. HerAgent's main contribution is semantic setup blocks: a single progress-control abstraction used for execution, validation, checkpointing, repair, and rollback. Evaluated against six prior agents on four environment-setup datasets, HerAgent improves setup success in every comparison, achieving the largest gains on Installamatic-Bench (52.0% to 85.0%) and SetupBench (46.3% to 70.4%). It also reduces setup costs by up to 94.5%, showing that block-level progress control improves reliability and efficiency.

title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
summary: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.
